syntax: SELECT o.id, (SELECT ... WHERE p.product = o.product ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1) AS cents FROM orders AS o
summary: Look up one related value separately for each row of an outer query.
documentation: A correlated subquery refers to columns of the outer row. Used as a scalar expression, it supplies one column from its first result row, or NULL if no row qualifies. Explicit ordering and LIMIT 1 make an as-of lookup deterministic.
inputs: orders(id, product, day) and prices(id, product, effective_day, cents); ids are distinct integer primary keys, all other columns are NOT NULL.
returns: order_id and the applicable cents, ordered by order_id; absent prices yield NULL.
caution: Filter by product and effective day before choosing the latest row. A scalar subquery that accidentally returns several rows silently uses the first in SQLite. Large production lookups need suitable indexes and a reviewed query plan.
scenarios: Show the price that applied on each historical order day.
Preview an effective-dated rate alongside imported transactions.
Attach the latest eligible configuration value while preserving rows with no match.
title: Find each order’s as-of price
problem: For each order, return its id AS order_id and the price cents from the same product with effective_day <= order day. Choose greatest effective_day, then greatest price id to break a tie. If none qualifies return NULL. Output by order_id.
hint: Correlate the product and day conditions to o, then order eligible prices descending and take one row.
goal: Use Correlated scalar subquery or an equivalent approach demonstrating the same premise.
